strengths: Well-motivated metric: VIG provides a principled, interpretable measure of visual contribution with clear mathematical formulation and proper theoretical grounding in information theory (KL divergence decomposition)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Tests across 7 benchmarks spanning vision understanding and hallucination, with 3 model variants, showing consistent improvements and robust ablations validating design choices
Practical data efficiency: Achieves better performance with substantially fewer training tokens (21-65% reduction depending on model), demonstrating the method's practical value
Complementary to existing approaches: Demonstrates orthogonality to inference-time (VCD, PAI, VAR) and training-based methods (LACING), with additive benefits when combined

Strong mechanistic validation: Clear evidence through attention analysis (Fig 4) and text-corruption experiments (Fig 5) that the method genuinely improves visual grounding rather than just optimizing benchmarks
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-structured paper with implementation details, hyperparameters, and qualitative examples enabling reproduction
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core contribution is relatively incremental—applying existing selective training principles (Lin et al. 2024) to LVLMs with a specific metric. The conceptual advance is modest

VIG's validity as ground truth is questionable: Perplexity changes reflect model prediction shifts, not necessarily semantic visual necessity. Blurred image approach for visual absence is an imperfect approximation; alternative visual nulling strategies not explored

Modest improvements across many metrics: LLaVAW 7B (+3.7%), MMVet 13B (+1.9%), DocVQA (+0.2-1.2%), and hallucination metrics show inconsistent gains; some improvements are small relative to typical training variance

Narrow architectural scope: Evaluation limited primarily to LLaVA variants with only one additional model (ShareGPT4V). Generalization to recent architectures (Qwen, DeepSeek, InternVL) unexplored; acknowledged but problematic for ICML submission

Significant computational overhead inadequately analyzed: VIG precomputation takes 6 hours on 8 RTX 4090s; total cost comparison with full-data training is missing. Claims about efficiency don't account for this preprocessing cost

Incomplete design justification: Reusing threshold τ_p at both sample and token levels justified only to avoid hyperparameters, but Table C.1 shows τ_p varies across models. No principled method for practitioners to select τ_p for new models

Missing critical analyses: No investigation of which sample types/domains are disproportionately filtered, no failure case analysis, no human evaluation of grounding quality, no sensitivity to blur parameters
Token-level masking under-analyzed: Computing loss only on selected tokens while maintaining full logits could introduce gradient flow biases; optimization implications not discussed

strengths: Well-grounded theoretical foundation with rigorous mathematical derivations connecting VIG to perplexity, cross-entropy loss, and KL divergence
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple architectures (4 model families) and extensive benchmarks covering both vision understanding and hallucination evaluation
Consistent performance improvements across all tested models with significant data efficiency gains (34-79% token reduction while maintaining or improving performance)
Excellent empirical analysis validating that VIG aligns with benchmark-level modality dependencies and successfully identifies visually grounded tokens vs. function words
Strong reproducibility with comprehensive implementation details, hyperparameters, training configurations, and honest discussion of computational overhead
Practical utility: architecture-agnostic approach requiring no model modifications and adding no inference overhead; demonstrates orthogonality to existing methods
Thorough ablation studies examining selection levels and ratios, with analysis of data distribution preservation showing long-tail concept retention
weaknesses: Visual absence simulation via Gaussian blur lacks sufficient justification; blur preserves spatial/structural information, and no empirical validation that it truly represents visual absence within the model's processing
Modest improvements on several benchmarks reduce practical significance (e.g., MMBench +0.87, DocVQA +0.20 for LLaVA-1.5 7B); no error bars or statistical significance testing reported

Hyperparameter choices appear pragmatic rather than principled: selection of p=70 lacks clear justification, and reusing τ_p at both sample/token levels is framed as avoiding hyperparameters rather than principled design
Limited architectural scope with experiments primarily on LLaVA-family models; generalization to recent architectures with different alignment strategies remains unclear
Computational overhead of VIG scoring (6 hours on 8 RTX 4090s) is non-negligible and could limit adoption, though framed as one-time cost; total cost-benefit analysis incomplete
Technical limitations: decomposition in Eq. 6 assumes token-level independence despite autoregressive dependencies; text-only samples left unchanged means method doesn't optimize this component
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multi-seed experiments reported; absence of direct comparisons with other data selection/valuation methods
